To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Hitchcock is right about the 1/2-1/3 disagreement, that the 1/4 answer to the Sleeping beauty problem is the right one, and that Hitchcock’s assumption is false.
Hitchcock’s argument fails and that Sleeping Beauty’s fair betting odds should be 1/2.

Hitchcock’s argument for a 1/3 credence for Sleeping Beauty fails because the assumption that credences track betting odds is false, that this assumption is false because of a peculiar feature of the Sleeping Beauty scenario, and that this peculiar feature of the scenario can be generalized to a wide class of scenarios, including a class of scenarios in which an agent is in the same epistemic situation as Sleeping Beauty, but is not in a dream.
In summary, our research is concerned with

a problem in the foundations of probability, namely how to calculate the credences of a rational agent in light of the betting odds that she is offered, and what this implies for the Sleeping Beauty problem and other cases of the kind.
the following question: when betting odds and credence come apart, what are the conditions under which they should be equal?
the following question: when is it rational for an agent to accept bets that are better than her fair betting odds?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
if the Sleeping Beauty scenario is a case of a Dutch book, then she should assign a credence of 1/3 to heads.
Sleeping Beauty should have a credence of 1/3 in heads, but she can only be justified in this credence if she is willing to accept a bet at odds better than 1/2.
Sleeping Beauty should bet 2:1 on Heads and 1:2 on Tails.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are arguing that there is a new condition for when an agent’s credence should track her fair odds of betting.
the Sleeping Beauty problem has a new answer, and a new way to solve it.
the Dutch Book Argument is not a good argument for the 1:1 answer to the Sleeping beauty problem, and it is not a good reason for believing that credences should follow fair betting odds.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is more to the Dutch book argument than has been previously thought.
the Dutch Book arguments for the Principal Principle are sensitive to the epistemic situation of the agents involved.
we have discovered a new condition that must be satisfied in order for an agent’s credences to follow her fair betting-odds.
